claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is thought to orchestrate cognitive dynamics.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is thought to orchestrate cognitive dynamics.
evidence: This is a general statement about the PFC's role in cognition, representing established scientific understanding.

claim: In tests of bistable visual perception, no direct evidence supporting causal roles of the PFC has been reported except for a recent work.
source: However, in tests of bistable visual perception, no direct evidence supporting such presumable causal roles of the PFC has been reported except for a recent work.
evidence: This statement references the state of the literature and cites a recent exception, drawing on existing research.

claim: Using a brain-state-dependent neural stimulation system, causal effects on percept dynamics were identified in three PFC activities: right frontal eye fields, dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC), and inferior frontal cortex (IFC).
source: Here, using a novel brain-state-dependent neural stimulation system, we identified causal effects on percept dynamics in three PFC activities—right frontal eye fields, dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC), and inferior frontal cortex (IFC).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from the main experiment.

claim: The causality is behaviourally detectable only when brain state dynamics are tracked and the PFC activity is modulated in brain-state-/state-history-dependent manners.
source: The causality is behaviourally detectable only when we track brain state dynamics and modulate the PFC activity in brain-state-/state-history-dependent manners.
evidence: This is a key finding from the experimental data showing state-dependent effects.

claim: The behavioural effects are underpinned by transient neural changes in the brain state dynamics.
source: The behavioural effects are underpinned by transient neural changes in the brain state dynamics, and such neural effects are quantitatively explainable by structural transformations of the hypothetical energy landscapes.
evidence: This is supported by the neural measurements and mediation analyses presented in the study.

claim: Neural effects are quantitatively explainable by structural transformations of the hypothetical energy landscapes.
source: The behavioural effects are underpinned by transient neural changes in the brain state dynamics, and such neural effects are quantitatively explainable by structural transformations of the hypothetical energy landscapes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations and correlations with empirical data.

claim: The DLPFC enhances the integration of two PFC-active brain states.
source: Moreover, these findings indicate distinct functions of the three PFC areas: in particular, the DLPFC enhances the integration of two PFC-active brain states, whereas IFC promotes the functional segregation between them.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing effects on energy barriers and brain state transitions.

claim: IFC promotes the functional segregation between two PFC-active brain states.
source: Moreover, these findings indicate distinct functions of the three PFC areas: in particular, the DLPFC enhances the integration of two PFC-active brain states, whereas IFC promotes the functional segregation between them.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing effects on energy barriers and brain state transitions.

claim: Bistable visual perception has been widely used to investigate cognitive dynamics.
source: Bistable visual perception has been widely used to investigate such cognitive dynamics (Brascamp et al., 2018; Sterzer et al., 2009), and the prefrontal cortex (PFC)—in particular, right frontal eye fields (FEF), dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) and inferior frontal cortex (IFC)—is thought to be involved in the spontaneous perceptual switching (Brascamp et al., 2018; Kleinschmidt et al., 1998; Lumer et al., 1998; Lumer and Rees, 1999; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2020; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012; Sterzer et al., 2009; Sterzer et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2013; Weilnhammer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The PFC (right FEF, DLPFC and IFC) is thought to be involved in spontaneous perceptual switching.
source: Bistable visual perception has been widely used to investigate such cognitive dynamics (Brascamp et al., 2018; Sterzer et al., 2009), and the prefrontal cortex (PFC)—in particular, right frontal eye fields (FEF), dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC) and inferior frontal cortex (IFC)—is thought to be involved in the spontaneous perceptual switching (Brascamp et al., 2018; Kleinschmidt et al., 1998; Lumer et al., 1998; Lumer and Rees, 1999; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2020; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012; Sterzer et al., 2009; Sterzer et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2013; Weilnhammer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Theoretical work indicates that top-down signals from the PFC to the visual cortex are essential to perceptual inference.
source: Theoretical work also indicates that top-down signals from the PFC to the visual cortex are essential to perceptual inference (Hohwy et al., 2008; Weilnhammer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: A recent work administering theta-burst transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the right IFC identified behavioural causality of the PFC.
source: However, no empirical human study has identified such behavioural causality of the PFC (Brascamp et al., 2018) except for a recent work administering theta-burst transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the right IFC (Weilnhammer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: A previous TMS study reported that neural suppression of the right DLPFC did not affect bistable visual perception.
source: Instead, a previous TMS study reported that neural suppression of the right DLPFC did not affect bistable visual perception (de Graaf et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Some studies claimed that the PFC activity is not essential to the emergence of multistable perception but merely a consequence of it.
source: Other studies claimed that the PFC activity is not essential to the emergence of multistable perception (Brascamp et al., 2015; Harrison and Tong, 2009) but mere a consequence of it (Block, 2020; Brascamp et al., 2015; Frässle et al., 2014; Knapen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Whole-brain neural activity during bistable perception is described as large-scale brain state dynamics.
source: Here, given that the whole-brain neural activity during bistable perception is described as large-scale brain state dynamics (Watanabe et al., 2014c), we hypothesise that causal roles of the PFC should also be dynamically changing during the fluctuation of visual awareness.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Causal roles of the PFC should be dynamically changing during the fluctuation of visual awareness.
source: Here, given that the whole-brain neural activity during bistable perception is described as large-scale brain state dynamics (Watanabe et al., 2014c), we hypothesise that causal roles of the PFC should also be dynamically changing during the fluctuation of visual awareness.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings and logical inference.

claim: The detectability of prefrontal causal effects on perceptual awareness should be determined by the brain state in which the neural activity pattern is staying when neural stimulation is administered.
source: That is, if the neural activity in the multistable perception can be stated as dwelling in and transitions between a parsimonious number of brain states (Watanabe et al., 2014c), the detectability of the prefrontal causal effects on the perceptual awareness should be determined by the brain state in which the neural activity pattern is staying when the neural stimulation is administered.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings and logical inference.

claim: State-dependent behavioural causality should be hardly observed when intervening in the PFC activity without tracking the brain state dynamics.
source: If so, such state-dependent behavioural causality should be hardly observed when we intervene in the PFC activity without tracking the brain state dynamics.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the hypothesis.

claim: A pairwise maximum entropy model was well fitted to the data in all participants with fitting accuracy >84%.
source: First, we confirmed that a pairwise maximum entropy model—a basis of the energy landscape analysis—was well fitted to the data in all the participants (fitting accuracy >84 %; Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: All participants had almost the same energy landscape structure consisting of three major brain states: Frontal-area-dominantly-active state (F state), Visual-area-dominantly-active state (V state) and Intermediate state (Int state).
source: Based on the model, we then found that all the participants had almost the same energy landscape structure consisting of three major brain states: Frontal-area-dominantly-active state (F state), Visual-area-dominantly-active state (V state) and Intermediate state (Int state) (e.g. Figure 2b for Participant 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2b and analysis results.

claim: The three brain states were significantly separated and independent from each other with energy barrier >1.
source: As in our previous fMRI work, these three states were significantly separated and independent from each other (i.e. the energy barrier >1; Figure 2c) and dominated almost all the energy surfaces (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The three major brain states dominated almost all the energy surfaces.
source: As in our previous fMRI work, these three states were significantly separated and independent from each other (i.e. the energy barrier >1; Figure 2c) and dominated almost all the energy surfaces (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Almost all neural activity patterns could be categorised into either of the three major brain states in the EEG data.
source: In the EEG data, almost all the neural activity patterns could be categorised into either of the three major brain states (e).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The basin sizes in the model accurately predicted the appearance frequency of the major brain states (r64 >0.57; MAPE < 6.8%).
source: The degree to which each of the three brain states occupied the energy landscape (i.e. the basin size) was significantly correlated with how frequently the brain state appeared in the EEG data (r64 >0.57; Mean Average Percentage Error, MAPE, < 6.8 %; Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: There was almost no direct transition between F and V state (<0.4%).
source: Moreover, the neural dynamics between these three major brain states were qualitatively equivalent to those seen in our fMRI study: there was almost no direct transition between F and V state ( < 0.4%; Figure 2g,h), and thus the brain activity pattern always used Int state as a stepping stone to travel between F and V state (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2g and 2h.

claim: The brain activity pattern always used Int state as a stepping stone to travel between F and V state.
source: Moreover, the neural dynamics between these three major brain states were qualitatively equivalent to those seen in our fMRI study: there was almost no direct transition between F and V state ( < 0.4%; Figure 2g,h), and thus the brain activity pattern always used Int state as a stepping stone to travel between F and V state (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is inferred from the transition data and illustrated in Figure 2i.

claim: The length of neural travel between F and V state via Int state was a good indicator to predict individual behavioural differences in percept duration (r64 = 0.67).
source: Finally, we confirmed that, as shown in our fMRI work, the length of such neural travel between F and V state via Int sate was a good indicator to predict the individual behavioural differences in the percept duration (r64 = 0.67; Figure 2j).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2j.

claim: The brain-behaviour association was preserved at an individual level: within each participant, the length of the F-Int-V-Int-F travel calculated for each run accurately predicted the percept duration in the run (r19 >0.54, MAPE <7.2%).
source: Furthermore, this brain-behaviour association was preserved at an individual level: even within each participant, the length of the F-Int-V-Int-F travel calculated for each run accurately predicted the percept duration in the run (e.g. Figure 2k for Participant 1; for all the participants, r19 >0.54, MAPE <7.2%, Figure 2l,m).
evidence: This is supported by the individual-level analysis shown in Figure 2k, 2l, and 2m.

claim: The brain state identification in the online analysis was significantly similar to that obtained by the offline analysis (similarity >82.3% for the three major brain states).
source: First, we confirmed that the brain state identification in the online analysis was significantly similar to that obtained by the offline analysis (similarity >82.3 % for the three major brain states; Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The system succeeded in triggering inhibitory TMS only when the neural activity pattern was staying in a specific major brain state (accuracy >84.8%, latency <0.8 ms).
source: Then, by linking this online EEG signal processing to monophasic TMS, we succeeded in triggering a burst of inhibitory TMS only when the neural activity pattern was staying in a specific major brain state (accuracy >84.8%, Figure 3b; latency <0.8 ms, Figure 3c).
evidence: This is supported by the accuracy and latency measurements shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: The three prefrontal areas had different causal behavioural effects on spontaneous perceptual switching in a brain-state-dependent manner (N = 34; F8,33=25.9, p < 10–3).
source: By applying this state-dependent TMS over the three PFC regions (i.e. DLPFC, IFC and FEF; Figure 4), we found that the three prefrontal areas had different causal behavioural effects on the spontaneous perceptual switching in a brain-state-dependent manner (N = 34; F8,33=25.9, p < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by the ANOVA results and data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Neural inhibition of DLPFC during F state prolonged the percept duration (t33 = 9.4, PBonferroni < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.7).
source: The neural inhibition of DLPFC during F state prolonged the percept duration (t33 = 9.4, PBonferroni < 0.001 in a post-hoc paired t-test, Cohen's d = 1.7), whereas that during V or Int state induced no behavioural change (t33 <1.7, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Neural inhibition of DLPFC during V or Int state induced no behavioural change (t33 <1.7, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.3).
source: The neural inhibition of DLPFC during F state prolonged the percept duration (t33 = 9.4, PBonferroni < 0.001 in a post-hoc paired t-test, Cohen's d = 1.7), whereas that during V or Int state induced no behavioural change (t33 <1.7, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: F-state-dependent TMS over IFC destabilised visual perception (t33 = 10.4, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 1.8).
source: Regarding IFC, the F-state-dependent TMS destabilised the visual perception (t33 = 10.4, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 1.8), whilst neither V- nor Int-state-dependent TMS induced any behavioural effect (t33 <1.3, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.29).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Neither V- nor Int-state-dependent TMS over IFC induced any behavioural effect (t33 <1.3, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.29).
source: Regarding IFC, the F-state-dependent TMS destabilised the visual perception (t33 = 10.4, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 1.8), whilst neither V- nor Int-state-dependent TMS induced any behavioural effect (t33 <1.3, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.29).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: F-state-dependent TMS over FEF reduced the percept duration (t33 = 10.5, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 1.9).
source: The F-state-dependent TMS over FEF reduced the percept duration (t33 = 10.5, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 1.9), whereas no behavioural change was observed in the other FEF TMS conditions (t33 <0.8, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.39).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: No behavioural change was observed in V- or Int-state-dependent FEF TMS conditions (t33 <0.8, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.39).
source: The F-state-dependent TMS over FEF reduced the percept duration (t33 = 10.5, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 1.9), whereas no behavioural change was observed in the other FEF TMS conditions (t33 <0.8, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.39).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: TMS over DLPFC during Int state immediately after F state shortened the percept duration (t33 = 12.9, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.7).
source: The TMS over DLPFC during Int state immediately after F state shortened the percept duration (t33 = 12.9, PBonferroni <0.001 in a post-hoc paired t-test, d = 2.7), whereas the TMS over DLPFC during Int state right after V state prolonged it (t33 = 13.3, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: TMS over DLPFC during Int state right after V state prolonged the percept duration (t33 = 13.3, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.3).
source: The TMS over DLPFC during Int state immediately after F state shortened the percept duration (t33 = 12.9, PBonferroni <0.001 in a post-hoc paired t-test, d = 2.7), whereas the TMS over DLPFC during Int state right after V state prolonged it (t33 = 13.3, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Post-F Int-state-dependent TMS over IFC enhanced perceptual stability (t33 = 9.1, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 1.6).
source: For IFC, the Post-F Int-state-dependent TMS enhanced the perceptual stability (t33 = 9.1, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 1.6), whilst that in Post-V Int state weakened it (t33 = 12.7, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Post-V Int-state-dependent TMS over IFC weakened perceptual stability (t33 = 12.7, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.3).
source: For IFC, the Post-F Int-state-dependent TMS enhanced the perceptual stability (t33 = 9.1, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 1.6), whilst that in Post-V Int state weakened it (t33 = 12.7, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.3).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: No change in percept duration was observed when TMS was administered over FEF during Post-F or Post-V Int state (t33 <0.58, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.19).
source: No change in the percept duration was observed when we administered TMS over FEF during Post-F or Post-V Int state (t33 <0.58, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.19).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: No significant behavioural change was induced by longer and stronger TMS (30 min quadripulse TMS with 90% AMT) over the same three PFC regions (N = 14; F2,13=0.16, p = 0.85).
source: Given that no significant behavioural change was induced by longer and stronger TMS (here, 30 min quadripulse TMS)(Hamada et al., 2009; Hamada et al., 2007; Watanabe et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 2014a) over the same PFC regions (N = 14; F2,13=0.16, p = 0.85 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; Figure 4d), these results suggest that the causal behavioural roles of the PFC areas in the bistable visual perception become explicit and measurable only when we intervene in the neural activity in state-/state-history-dependent manners.
evidence: This is supported by the ANOVA results and data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The causal behavioural roles of the PFC areas in bistable visual perception become explicit and measurable only when intervening in the neural activity in state-/state-history-dependent manners.
source: Given that no significant behavioural change was induced by longer and stronger TMS (here, 30 min quadripulse TMS)(Hamada et al., 2009; Hamada et al., 2007; Watanabe et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 2014a) over the same PFC regions (N = 14; F2,13=0.16, p = 0.85 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; Figure 4d), these results suggest that the causal behavioural roles of the PFC areas in the bistable visual perception become explicit and measurable only when we intervene in the neural activity in state-/state-history-dependent manners.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between state-dependent and conventional TMS results.

claim: TMS over DLPFC increased the energy barrier heights between F and Int state (F4,33=340.1, p < 10–3; t33 >15.2, PBonferroni <0.001, d > 2.6).
source: As to DLPFC (Figure 5b), the numerical simulation showed that the TMS should increase the energy barrier heights between F and Int state (F4,33=340.1, p < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; t33 >15.2, PBonferroni <0.001 in post-hoc paired t-tests, d > 2.6) and decrease the barrier height from Int to V state (t33 = 38.0, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 6.7).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulation results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: TMS over DLPFC decreased the barrier height from Int to V state (t33 = 38.0, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 6.7).
source: As to DLPFC (Figure 5b), the numerical simulation showed that the TMS should increase the energy barrier heights between F and Int state (F4,33=340.1, p < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; t33 >15.2, PBonferroni <0.001 in post-hoc paired t-tests, d > 2.6) and decrease the barrier height from Int to V state (t33 = 38.0, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 6.7).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulation results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: TMS over DLPFC significantly increased the ratio of the Int-to-F barrier to the Int-to-V barrier (t33 = 27.1, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 4.8).
source: As a result, the ratio of the Int-to-F barrier to the Int-to-V barrier should significantly increase (t33 = 27.1, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 4.8).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulation results.

claim: Neural inhibition of IFC alleviated the energy barriers between F and Int state (F4,33=89.10, p < 10–3; t33 >11.6, PBonferroni <0.001, d > 2.0).
source: Regarding IFC (Figure 5c), the neural inhibition of the region should alleviate the energy barriers between F and Int state (F4,33=89.10, p < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; t33 >11.6, PBonferroni <0.001, d > 2.0) and that from Int to V state (t33 = 48.9, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 8.6).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulation results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Neural inhibition of IFC alleviated the energy barrier from Int to V state (t33 = 48.9, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 8.6).
source: Regarding IFC (Figure 5c), the neural inhibition of the region should alleviate the energy barriers between F and Int state (F4,33=89.10, p < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; t33 >11.6, PBonferroni <0.001, d > 2.0) and that from Int to V state (t33 = 48.9, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 8.6).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulation results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: TMS over IFC resulted in a significant decrease in the ratio of the Int-to-F barrier to the Int-to-V barrier (t33 = 61.2, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 10.7).
source: The magnitude of the decrease in the Int-to-F barrier height should become larger than that in the Int-to-V barrier, which would result in a significant decrease in the ratio of the Int-to-F barrier to the Int-to-V barrier (t33 = 61.2, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 10.7).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulation results.

claim: Neural suppression of FEF lowered the energy barrier from F to Int state (F4,33=32.4, p < 10–3; t33=25.3, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 4.4).
source: For FEF (Figure 5d), its neural suppression should lower the energy barrier from F to Int state (F4,33=32.4, p < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; t33=25.3, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 4.4) but induce no significant change in the other barriers (t33 <1.7, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.27).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulation results shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Neural suppression of FEF induced no significant change in energy barriers other than F-to-Int (t33 <1.7, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.27).
source: For FEF (Figure 5d), its neural suppression should lower the energy barrier from F to Int state (F4,33=32.4, p < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; t33=25.3, PBonferroni < 0.001, d = 4.4) but induce no significant change in the other barriers (t33 <1.7, PBonferroni > 0.05, d < 0.27).
evidence: This is based on numerical simulation results shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The increase in the F-to-Int energy barrier after TMS over DLPFC was correlated with longer F-state dwelling in F-state-dependent TMS (t33 = 11.6, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.0; r33 = 0.59, p < 0.001).
source: In the experiments administering TMS over DLPFC, the increase in the F-to-Int energy barrier was correlated with the longer F-state dwelling seen in the F-state-dependent TMS (t33 = 11.6, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.0; r33 = 0.59, p < 0.001; Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The higher Int-to-F energy barrier after TMS over DLPFC was associated with more frequent Int-to-V transitions in Int-state-dependent TMS (t33 = 3.3, PBonferroni <0.05, d = 1.8; r33 = 0.52, p < 0.001).
source: Also, the higher Int-to-F energy barrier was associated with more frequent Int-to-V transitions that was seen in the Int-state-dependent TMS (t33 = 3.3, PBonferroni <0.05, d = 1.8; r33 = 0.52, p < 0.001; Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The lower F-to-Int energy barrier after TMS over IFC was correlated with shorter F-state dwelling in F-state-dependent neural suppression (t33 = 6.9, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 1.2; r33 = 0.69, p < 0.001).
source: In the sessions administering TMS over IFC, the lower F-to-I energy barrier was correlated with the shorter F-state dwelling that was measured in the F-state-dependent neural suppression (t33 = 6.9, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 1.2; r33 = 0.69, p < 0.001; Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The lower Int-to-F barrier after TMS over IFC accurately predicted more frequent Int-to-F transitions (t33 = 13.0, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.8; r33=–0.58, p < 0.001).
source: The lower Int-to-F barrier accurately predicted more frequent Int-to-F transitions (t33 = 13.0, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 2.8; r33=–0.58, p < 0.001; Figure 6e) that were seen in the Int-state-dependent TMS condition.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The lower F-to-Int barrier after TMS over FEF was associated with shorter F-state dwelling in F-state-dependent TMS session (t33 = 26.1, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 4.8; r33 = 0.57, p < 0.001).
source: In the TMS-over-FEF conditions, the lower F-to-Int barrier was associated with the shorter F-state dwelling that was observed in the F-state-dependent TMS session (t33 = 26.1, PBonferroni <0.001, d = 4.8; r33 = 0.57, p < 0.001; Figure 6f).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: All correlations between neural effects and energy barrier changes began to weaken approximately 1.5 s after each TMS.
source: This analysis detected that all the correlations began to weaken approximately 1.5 s after each TMS (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by the temporal analysis shown in Figure 7b.

claim: The TMS-induced neural effects started to decay within ~1.5 s after the stimulation, and the brain state dynamics began to return to the original forms in such a time scale.
source: This result indicates that the current TMS-induced neural effects started to decay within ~1.5 s after the stimulation, and the brain state dynamics began to return to the original forms in such a time scale.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal decay analysis.

claim: The causal behavioural effects are induced by transient changes in the brain state dynamics and attributable to structural changes in the energy landscapes (P < 0.05 for all indirect effects, α×β).
source: Finally, we evaluated associations between these behavioural, numerical and neural responses by mediation analysis and found that the causal behavioural effects are induced by transient changes in the brain state dynamics and attributable to structural changes in the energy landscapes (P < 0.05 for all the indirect effects, α×β; Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The longer percept duration after F-state-dependent TMS over DLPFC was largely due to prolonged F-state dwelling, which was induced by the higher F-to-Int energy barrier.
source: As to the state-dependent behavioural changes, the longer percept duration seen after the F-state-dependent TMS over DLPFC was largely due to the prolonged F-state dwelling, which was induced by the higher F-to-Int energy barrier (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The de-stabilisation of visual perception after F-state-dependent TMS over IFC/FEF was caused by shorter F-state dwelling, which was attributable to the lower F-to-Int energy barrier.
source: In contrast, the de-stabilisation of visual perception seen after the F-state-dependent TMS over IFC/FEF was caused by the shorter F-state dwelling, which was attributable to the lower F-to-Int energy barrier (Figure 8b,c).
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis shown in Figure 8b and 8c.

claim: The shorter percept duration after Post-F Int-state-dependent TMS over DLPFC was caused by increased Int-to-V transitions, which was triggered by the larger gap between Int-to-F and Int-to-V barriers.
source: According to the mediation analysis, the shorter percept duration seen after the Post-F Int-state-dependent TMS over DLPFC was caused by the increase in the Int-to-V transitions, which was triggered by the larger gap between the Int-to-F barrier and Int-to-V barrier (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis shown in Figure 8d.

claim: The longer percept duration after Post-V Int-state-dependent TMS over DLPFC is interpretable as a result of the relatively higher Int-to-F energy barrier impeding Int-to-F transitions, accelerating backward moves to V state and slowing down completion of the F-Int-V travel.
source: Conversely, the longer percept duration yielded by the Post-V Int-state-dependent TMS over DLPFC is interpretable as a result of the relatively higher Int-to-F energy barrier's impeding the Int-to-F transitions, accelerating the backward moves to V state and slowing down the completion of the F-Int-V travel (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis shown in Figure 8e.

claim: The longer percept duration after TMS over IFC during Post-F Int state could be regarded as a behavioural manifestation of the slowdown of the F-Int-V travel due to more frequent backward Int-to-F transitions, which originated from the relatively lower Int-to-F energy barrier.
source: The mediation analysis showed that the state-history-dependent causal roles of IFC were also accountable by the same logic. The longer percept duration yielded by the TMS over IFC during Post-F Int state could be regarded as a behavioural manifestation of the slowdown of the F-Int-V travel due to the more frequent backward Int-to-F transitions, which was originated from the relatively lower Int-to-F energy barrier (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis shown in Figure 8f.

claim: The shorter percept duration induced by TMS over IFC during Post-V Int state can be seen as results of the acceleration of the F-Int-V travel due to more frequent forward moves from Int to F state, which was induced by the lower Int-to-F energy barrier.
source: In contrast, the shorter percept duration induced by the TMS over IFC during Post-V Int state can be seen as results of the acceleration of the F-Int-V travel due to the more frequent forward moves from Int to F state, which was induced by the lower Int-to-F energy barrier (Figure 8g).
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis shown in Figure 8g.

claim: All main behavioural findings were replicated in an independent cohort (N = 14; t13 >2.9, P < 0.01).
source: The main behavioural findings were replicated in a small but independent cohort (N = 14; t13 >2.9, P < 0.01 in one-sample t-tests; Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by the replication data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: Excitatory TMS induced behavioural effects opposite to those yielded by inhibitory stimulation (t14 >2.8, P < 0.01).
source: Moreover, another independent experiment (N = 15) showed that, as in our previous work (Watanabe et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 2014a), the excitatory TMS induced behavioural effects opposite to those yielded by the inhibitory stimulation (t14 >2.8, P < 0.01 in one-sample t-tests; Figure 9b), which added indirect but empirical support for the current observations.
evidence: This is supported by the validation experiment data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: The behavioural effects of state-/state-history-dependent TMS became larger along with weekly TMS sessions (t12 >3.2, PBonferroni < 0.05).
source: To examine the potential of future clinical applications of this brain-state-dependent neural stimulation system, we conducted another two-month longitudinal experiment (N = 63) and found accumulative effects of this closed-loop TMS system. Despite its weak power—approximately 78 % of the power of the similar TMS protocol (Watanabe et al., 2015; Watanabe et al., 2014a)—, the behavioural effects became larger along with the weekly TMS sessions (t12 >3.2, PBonferroni < 0.05 in paired t-tests; Figure 10a).
evidence: This is supported by the longitudinal data shown in Figure 10a.

claim: F-state-dependent TMS affected the baseline perceptual stability, which was detectable even one week after the 2-month TMS experiments (F6,12=16.4, P < 10–3; PBonferroni < 0.01).
source: Moreover, the F-state-dependent TMS affected the baseline perceptual stability, which was detectable even one week after the 2-month TMS experiments (F6,12=16.4, P < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; PBonferroni < 0.01 in post-hoc one-sample t-tests; Figure 10b).
evidence: This is supported by the longitudinal data shown in Figure 10b.

claim: The activation of DLPFC enhances the functional integration between the Frontal and Intermediate state.
source: This study has demonstrated that causal roles of the three PFC regions—right DLPFC, IFC and FEF—in spontaneous perceptual inference were behaviourally detectable when we tracked the brain state dynamics underpinning such perceptual fluctuation. The state-/state-history-dependent behavioural causality was explained by the large-scale brain state dynamics and attributable to the energy landscape structures. Moreover, the current findings suggest distinct functions of the PFC regions in terms of the brain state dynamics: the activation of DLPFC enhances the functional integration between the Frontal and Intermediate state, whereas the IFC activity promotes the functional segregation between the two brain states; the FEF activity stabilises Frontal state.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings on energy barriers and brain state transitions.

claim: In SFM-induced bistable perception, the higher order cortex is considered to be more involved in the perceptual fluctuation compared to binocular rivalry.
source: To focus on the higher order cortex, we did not adopt a test of binocular rivalry, in which the perceptual fluctuation has often been linked with the neural activity in the lower level brain systems such as the visual cortex (Haynes et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2005; Leopold and Logothetis, 1996; Meng and Tong, 2004; Miller et al., 2000; Pettigrew and Miller, 1998; Polonsky et al., 2000). Instead, we used a test of bistable visual perception induced by a structure-from-motion (SFM) stimulus (Figure 1a), in which the same visual stimulus is presented to both the eyes of participants, and the higher order cortex is considered to be more involved in the perceptual fluctuation (Brascamp et al., 2018; Knapen et al., 2011; Meng and Tong, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research comparing different types of bistable perception.

claim: The current EEG system captured qualitatively the same brain state dynamics as those found in previous fMRI study employing the same SFM stimulus.
source: As a preparation, we examined whether the current EEG system captured qualitatively the same brain state dynamics as those found in our previous fMRI study employing the same SFM stimulus (Watanabe et al., 2014c).
evidence: This is supported by the validation analyses comparing EEG and fMRI results.

claim: The proportion of mixture perception was sufficiently small in all participants (1.4% ± 0.5% of all stimulus presentation times).
source: The proportion of the mixture perception was sufficiently small in all the participants, all the experiments (1.4% ± 0.5% of all stimulus presentation times, mean ± sd).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the experiments.

claim: 65 healthy adults participated in the control experiments.
source: To this end, we recorded gamma-band EEG signals from the seven cortical regions (Watanabe et al., 2014c; Figure 1b) of 65 healthy adults while they were experiencing the SFM-induced bistable visual perception (left panel of Figure 1c) and applied an offline energy landscape analysis to the data (Control Experiment I).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: The sample size of the main experiment was 34 participants.
source: By applying this state-dependent TMS over the three PFC regions (i.e. DLPFC, IFC and FEF; Figure 4), we found that the three prefrontal areas had different causal behavioural effects on the spontaneous perceptual switching in a brain-state-dependent manner (N = 34; F8,33=25.9, p < 10–3 for the main effect in a two-way ANOVA; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants in the main experiment.
